function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

{"content": "     1|# Week 12: Days 78-84 Postpartum
     2|
     3|## Body: Maternal Recovery & Breastfeeding/Pumping
     4|
     5|By week 12 postpartum, your body has made remarkable progress in healing from pregnancy and delivery. Most physical recovery is complete, though some changes may persist. You're likely settling into a more predictable routine with your baby, but new challenges may arise as you consider returning to work or adjust to life as a family of three.
     6|
     7|**Physical Recovery Status**:
     8|- Uterus has returned to near pre-pregnancy size and position
     9|- Lochia should have completely stopped by now (any persistent bleeding warrants evaluation)
    10|- Perineal healing is complete for vaginal deliveries; C-section incisions are well-healed
    11|- Hormone levels continue to stabilize, though prolactin remains elevated if breastfeeding
    12|- Many experience the return of menstrual cycles around this time, especially if not exclusively breastfeeding
    13|
    14|**Breastfeeding & Pumping Considerations**:
    15|At 3 months, breastfeeding patterns are typically well-established. If you're returning to work, this is often when pumping routines become crucial.
    16|
    17|> "I was terrified of dropping my supply when I went back to work" — Signal from r/breastfeeding
    18|
    19|If pumping for work:
    20|- Aim to pump every 3 hours while separated from baby to maintain supply
    21|- Store milk properly: fresh breastmilk lasts 4 hours at room temperature, 4 days in refrigerator, 6-12 months in freezer
    22|- Consider hands-free pumping bras to maximize efficiency during pumping sessions
    23|- Power pumping (pumping on and off for an hour) can help boost supply if needed
    24|
    25|If exclusively breastfeeding:
    26|- Feedings may become more efficient, often taking 10-15 minutes per breast
    27|- Baby likely takes larger volumes less frequently (every 3-4 hours during day)
    28|- Night feedings may decrease to 1-2 times per night for many babies
    29|
    30|**Nutrition & Self-Care**:
    31|- Continue prenatal vitamins while breastfeeding
    32|- Focus on nutrient-dense foods to support healing and energy needs
    33|- Hydration remains crucial, especially if breastfeeding/pumping
    34|- Gentle core exercises can begin if diastasis recti has improved (consult PT if separation >2 fingers)
    35|- Pelvic floor physical therapy is beneficial for many postpartum individuals
    36|
    37|## Baby: Development & Care at 3 Months
    38|
    39|Your baby is now 3 months old—a major milestone! The "fourth trimester" is ending, and you're seeing more of their personality emerge.
    40|
    41|**Developmental Milestones**:
    42|- Begins to push up on arms during tummy time (holding head steady)
    43|- Opens and closes hands, brings hands to mouth
    44|- Swipes at dangling objects with hands
    45|- Follows moving objects with eyes from side to side
    46|- Recognizes familiar faces and people at a distance
    47|- Begins to babble and mimic some sounds
    48|- Smiles spontaneously, especially at people
    49|
    50|**Sleep Patterns**:
    51|- Total sleep: 12-15 hours per day (including naps)
    52|- Night sleep may consolidate to longer stretches (4-6 hours for some)
    53|- Still takes 3-4 naps per day, typically 30 minutes to 2 hours each
    54|- Sleep regressions can occur around this time due to developmental leaps
    55|- Begin establishing a simple bedtime routine (bath, book, feed, bed)
    56|
    57|**Feeding**:
    58|- Breastfed babies: typically 5-6 feeds per day
    59|- Formula-fed: approximately 24-32 oz per day spread over 5-6 feeds
    60|- Feeding becomes more efficient and predictable
    61|- May show interest in your food (though solids not recommended until 4-6 months)
    62|- Continue vitamin D supplementation if breastfeeding (400 IU daily)
    63|
    64|**Soothing & Play**:
    65|- Enjoys gentle play: talking, singing, reading simple books
    66|- Responds to facial expressions and tone of voice
    67|- May self-soothe by sucking on hands
    68|- Enjoys gentle rocking, walking, or vibration for calming
    69|- Tummy time remains important for development (aim for 20-30 minutes daily total)
    70|
    71|## Mental Health: Navigating the New Normal
    72|
    73|At 3 months postpartum, many experience a shift from the intense newborn period to a more settled routine—but new emotional challenges can emerge.
    74|
    75|> "I feel like I'm losing myself" — Signal from Quora (common theme in maternal identity discussions)
    76|
    77|**Common Experiences**:
    78|- Relief that the most intense newborn phase is passing
    79|- Potential resurgence of anxiety about returning to work or leaving baby
    80|- Body image concerns as pregnancy changes persist
    81|- Relationship adjustments as focus shifts from survival to reconnection
    82|- Grief for pre-baby life or identity (completely normal)
    83|- Increased confidence in parenting abilities
    84|
    85|**When to Seek Additional Support**:
    86|While the "baby blues" should have resolved by now, persistent mood symptoms warrant attention:
    87|- Feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or emptiness most days for >2 weeks
    88|- Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you once enjoyed
    89|- Significant changes in appetite or sleep (beyond newborn-related)
    90|- Overwhelming guilt or feelings of inadequacy as a mother
    91|- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby (seek immediate help)
    92|- Panic attacks or persistent worry that feels uncontrollable
    93|
    94|**Coping Strategies for This Stage**:
    95|- Schedule brief "check-ins" with yourself: How am I *really* doing today?
    96|- Maintain social connections—adult conversation is vital
    97|- Celebrate small victories in your parenting journey
    98|- Allow yourself to feel complex emotions without judgment
    99|- Consider therapy specializing in perinatal mental health if symptoms persist
   100|- Communicate openly with your partner about changing needs and expectations
   101|
   102|## Partner Playbook: Supporting the 3-Month Transition
   103|
   104|Your partner's role evolves as you move beyond survival mode into establishing your family rhythm.
   105|
   106|**If You're Returning to Work**:
   107|- Handle morning routine: dress baby, pack diaper bag, prepare bottles if needed
   108|- Take over evening feeding/pumping cleanup and sterilization
   109|- Manage milk storage system: labeling, organizing freezer stash
   110|- Handle daycare drop-off/pickup if applicable
   111|- Be flexible with schedule for pumping breaks or unexpected baby needs
   112|
   113|**Continued Daily Support**:
   114|- Share nighttime responsibilities: even if baby sleeps longer stretches, take turns with early morning wakings
   115|- Initiate one-on-one time with baby: bath time, walks, play sessions
   116|- Take charge of at least one daily chore completely (laundry, dishes, meal prep)
   117|- Plan regular "adult time"—even 15 minutes to talk without baby focus
   118|- Notice and acknowledge what you're doing well as a parent
   119|
   120|**Emotional Connection**:
   121|- Check in regularly: "How are you feeling about work/baby/us lately?"
   122|- Plan mini-dates: coffee together while baby naps, walk around the block
   123|- Leave appreciative notes for each other
   124|- Attend pediatrician visits together when possible to stay aligned on baby's health
   125|- Remember: showing up consistently matters more than grand gestures
   126|
   127|> "Partner involvement drops off after newborn phase but is crucial long-term" — Signal insight from dossier
   128|
   129|## Call Doctor? Red-Flag Table for Week 12
   130|
   131||| Symptom | Normal | When to Call |
   132|||---------|--------|--------------|
   133||| **Bleeding** | Lochia should have stopped completely by 4-6 weeks postpartum. | Any vaginal bleeding after 6 weeks (could indicate retained products, hormonal issues, or other pathology) |
   134||| **Perineal/C-Section Pain** | All surgical/perineal pain should be resolved by 8-12 weeks. | Persistent or worsening pain, signs of infection (redness, swelling, pus, foul odor), or pain interfering with daily activities |
   135||| **Breast Issues** | If breastfeeding: comfortable feeds, no pain. If weaning: gradual decrease in milk production. | Red streaks, fever, flu-like symptoms (mastitis); severe engorgement not relieved by feeding/pumping; lump that doesn't move or resolve in 1-2 weeks |
   136||| **Baby's Growth & Feeding** | Steady weight gain, content after feeds, appropriate wet/dirty diapers | Poor weight gain, projectile vomiting, bloody/mucousy stool, extreme lethargy or irritability, refusing multiple feeds in a row |
   137||| **Baby's Development** | Smiles, coos, head control improving, follows objects with eyes | Not tracking objects with eyes by 3 months, not responding to loud sounds, not smiling at people, not bringing hands to mouth |
   138||| **Mental Health** | Occasional worry or sadness, mostly enjoying baby and parenting journey | Persistent sadness/anxiety >2 weeks, inability to cope with daily tasks, thoughts of self-harm or harming baby, hallucinations or delusions |
   139||| **Energy Levels** | Tired but functional, able to rest when baby sleeps | Exhaustion that doesn't improve with rest, inability to get out of bed, loss of all interest in previously enjoyed activities |
   140||| **Pelvic Floor** | Occasional leakage with cough/sneeze improving, pelvic pressure decreasing | Urinary/fecal incontinence that worsens or doesn't improve, bulging sensation in vagina, difficulty emptying bladder/bowels |
   141||| **Headaches** | Occasional tension headaches related to fatigue/posture | Severe headaches, vision changes, headaches with fever/stiff neck, headaches worsening or not responding to treatment |
   142||| **Thyroid Function** | Gradual return to pre-pregnancy energy levels | Persistent fatigue, weight changes, hair loss, temperature intolerance, rapid heartbeat (could indicate postpartum thyroiditis) |
   143|
   144|**Remember**: When in doubt, call your provider. It's always better to check.
   145|
   146|---
   147|*This week's guidance is based on:*
   148|- *ACOG Practice Bulletin: Postpartum Care*
   149|- *ACOG Committee Opinion: Optimizing Postpartum Care*
   150|- *AAP Bright Futures: Guidelines for Health Supervision of Infants*
   151|- *WHO Guidelines on Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health*
   152|- *US Preventive Services Task Force: Depression in Adults Screening*
   153|- *Signal data from 83+ Reddit, Quora, and YouTube posts reflecting real maternal experiences*
   154|- *La Leche League International: Breastfeeding Answers Made Simple*
   155|
   156|*Looking ahead: Week 13 will cover navigating sleep regressions, introducing solids preparation, and maintaining your relationship as parents.*", "total_lines": 155, "file_size": 9936, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false}

{"text": "# Week 12: Days 78-84 Postpartum

## Body: Maternal Recovery & Breastfeeding/Pumping

By week 12 postpartum, your body has made remarkable progress in healing from pregnancy and delivery. Most physical recovery is complete, though some changes may persist. You're likely settling into a more predictable routine with your baby, but new challenges may arise as you consider returning to work or adjust to life as a family of three.

**Physical Recovery Status**:
- Uterus has returned to near pre-pregnancy size and position
- Lochia should have completely stopped by now (any persistent bleeding warrants evaluation)
- Perineal healing is complete for vaginal deliveries; C-section incisions are well-healed
- Hormone levels continue to stabilize, though prolactin remains elevated if breastfeeding
- Many experience the return of menstrual cycles around this time, especially if not exclusively breastfeeding

**Breastfeeding & Pumping Considerations**:
At 3 months, breastfeeding patterns are typically well-established. If you're returning to work, this is often when pumping routines become crucial.

> "I was terrified of dropping my supply when I went back to work" — Signal from r/breastfeeding

If pumping for work:
- Aim to pump every 3 hours while separated from baby to maintain supply
- Store milk properly: fresh breastmilk lasts 4 hours at room temperature, 4 days in refrigerator, 6-12 months in freezer
- Consider hands-free pumping bras to maximize efficiency during pumping sessions
- Power pumping (pumping on and off for an hour) can help boost supply if needed

If exclusively breastfeeding:
- Feedings may become more efficient, often taking 10-15 minutes per breast
- Baby likely takes larger volumes less frequently (every 3-4 hours during day)
- Night feedings may decrease to 1-2 times per night for many babies

**Nutrition & Self-Care**:
- Continue prenatal vitamins while breastfeeding
- Focus on nutrient-dense foods to support healing and energy needs
- Hydration remains crucial, especially if breastfeeding/pumping
- Gentle core exercises can begin if diastasis recti has improved (consult PT if separation >2 fingers)
- Pelvic floor physical therapy is beneficial for many postpartum individuals

## Baby: Development & Care at 3 Months

Your baby is now 3 months old—a major milestone! The "fourth trimester" is ending, and you're seeing more of their personality emerge.

**Developmental Milestones**:
- Begins to push up on arms during tummy time (holding head steady)
- Opens and closes hands, brings hands to mouth
- Swipes at dangling objects with hands
- Follows moving objects with eyes from side to side
- Recognizes familiar faces and people at a distance
- Begins to babble and mimic some sounds
- Smiles spontaneously, especially at people

**Sleep Patterns**:
- Total sleep: 12-15 hours per day (including naps)
- Night sleep may consolidate to longer stretches (4-6 hours for some)
- Still takes 3-4 naps per day, typically 30 minutes to 2 hours each
- Sleep regressions can occur around this time due to developmental leaps
- Begin establishing a simple bedtime routine (bath, book, feed, bed)

**Feeding**:
- Breastfed babies: typically 5-6 feeds per day
- Formula-fed: approximately 24-32 oz per day spread over 5-6 feeds
- Feeding becomes more efficient and predictable
- May show interest in your food (though solids not recommended until 4-6 months)
- Continue vitamin D supplementation if breastfeeding (400 IU daily)

**Soothing & Play**:
- Enjoys gentle play: talking, singing, reading simple books
- Responds to facial expressions and tone of voice
- May self-soothe by sucking on hands
- Enjoys gentle rocking, walking, or vibration for calming
- Tummy time remains important for development (aim for 20-30 minutes daily total)

## Mental Health: Navigating the New Normal

At 3 months postpartum, many experience a shift from the intense newborn period to a more settled routine—but new emotional challenges can emerge.

> "I feel like I'm losing myself" — Signal from Quora (common theme in maternal identity discussions)

**Common Experiences**:
- Relief that the most intense newborn phase is passing
- Potential resurgence of anxiety about returning to work or leaving baby
- Body image concerns as pregnancy changes persist
- Relationship adjustments as focus shifts from survival to reconnection
- Grief for pre-baby life or identity (completely normal)
- Increased confidence in parenting abilities

**When to Seek Additional Support**:
While the "baby blues" should have resolved by now, persistent mood symptoms warrant attention:
- Feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or emptiness most days for >2 weeks
- Loss of interest or pleasure in activities you once enjoyed
- Significant changes in appetite or sleep (beyond newborn-related)
- Overwhelming guilt or feelings of inadequacy as a mother
- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby (seek immediate help)
- Panic attacks or persistent worry that feels uncontrollable

**Coping Strategies for This Stage**:
- Schedule brief "check-ins" with yourself: How am I *really* doing today?
- Maintain social connections—adult conversation is vital
- Celebrate small victories in your parenting journey
- Allow yourself to feel complex emotions without judgment
- Consider therapy specializing in perinatal mental health if symptoms persist
- Communicate openly with your partner about changing needs and expectations

## Partner Playbook: Supporting the 3-Month Transition

Your partner's role evolves as you move beyond survival mode into establishing your family rhythm.

**If You're Returning to Work**:
- Handle morning routine: dress baby, pack diaper bag, prepare bottles if needed
- Take over evening feeding/pumping cleanup and sterilization
- Manage milk storage system: labeling, organizing freezer stash
- Handle daycare drop-off/pickup if applicable
- Be flexible with schedule for pumping breaks or unexpected baby needs

**Continued Daily Support**:
- Share nighttime responsibilities: even if baby sleeps longer stretches, take turns with early morning wakings
- Initiate one-on-one time with baby: bath time, walks, play sessions
- Take charge of at least one daily chore completely (laundry, dishes, meal prep)
- Plan regular "adult time"—even 15 minutes to talk without baby focus
- Notice and acknowledge what you're doing well as a parent

**Emotional Connection**:
- Check in regularly: "How are you feeling about work/baby/us lately?"
- Plan mini-dates: coffee together while baby naps, walk around the block
- Leave appreciative notes for each other
- Attend pediatrician visits together when possible to stay aligned on baby's health
- Remember: showing up consistently matters more than grand gestures

> "Partner involvement drops off after newborn phase but is crucial long-term" — Signal insight from dossier

## Call Doctor? Red-Flag Table for Week 12

||| Symptom | Normal | When to Call |
|||---------|--------|--------------|
||| **Bleeding** | Lochia should have stopped completely by 4-6 weeks postpartum. | Any vaginal bleeding after 6 weeks (could indicate retained products, hormonal issues, or other pathology) |
||| **Perineal/C-Section Pain** | All surgical/perineal pain should be resolved by 8-12 weeks. | Persistent or worsening pain, signs of infection (redness, swelling, pus, foul odor), or pain interfering with daily activities |
||| **Breast Issues** | If breastfeeding: comfortable feeds, no pain. If weaning: gradual decrease in milk production. | Red streaks, fever, flu-like symptoms (mastitis); severe engorgement not relieved by feeding/pumping; lump that doesn't move or resolve in 1-2 weeks |
||| **Baby's Growth & Feeding** | Steady weight gain, content after feeds, appropriate wet/dirty diapers | Poor weight gain, projectile vomiting, bloody/mucousy stool, extreme lethargy or irritability, refusing multiple feeds in a row |
||| **Baby's Development** | Smiles, coos, head control improving, follows objects with eyes | Not tracking objects with eyes by 3 months, not responding to loud sounds, not smiling at people, not bringing hands to mouth |
||| **Mental Health** | Occasional worry or sadness, mostly enjoying baby and parenting journey | Persistent sadness/anxiety >2 weeks, inability to cope with daily tasks, thoughts of self-harm or harming baby, hallucinations or delusions |
||| **Energy Levels** | Tired but functional, able to rest when baby sleeps | Exhaustion that doesn't improve with rest, inability to get out of bed, loss of all interest in previously enjoyed activities |
||| **Pelvic Floor** | Occasional leakage with cough/sneeze improving, pelvic pressure decreasing | Urinary/fecal incontinence that worsens or doesn't improve, bulging sensation in vagina, difficulty emptying bladder/bowels |
||| **Headaches** | Occasional tension headaches related to fatigue/posture | Severe headaches, vision changes, headaches with fever/stiff neck, headaches worsening or not responding to treatment |
||| **Thyroid Function** | Gradual return to pre-pregnancy energy levels | Persistent fatigue, weight changes, hair loss, temperature intolerance, rapid heartbeat (could indicate postpartum thyroiditis) |

**Remember**: When in doubt, call your provider. It's always better to check.
